title: The Chaos Monkey

post.author: u/quernmoor_nights_nokuthula
post.title: I'm a night keeper at a zoo. At 02:10:30 the bolt of the big-cat house's keeper door slid back. Nobody had touched a card.

blocks.text: I'm Nokuthula, night keeper at Quernmoor Zoo. After closing I walk the keeper corridors behind the animal houses. Each house has a keeper door that opens only to a keeper's card.

The doors take orders from a small computer in the workshop, called a door controller. The orders go by radio through a box on the roof, called the hub. The north hub reaches four keeper doors: big-cat house, ape house, reptile house, feed store.
There are two controllers, a main and a backup. The main claims each door, one at a time, then tells them all 'all well' every 5 seconds. A door counts that only from the controller that claimed it.
Every two minutes, on the even minute, the main claims every door again: the roll call.
The doors keep one fire rule: after 30 seconds with no 'all well' from its controller, a door unlocks, so no keeper is shut inside a burning house.
A controller being switched off says one last thing to its group of doors: 'controller down'. Each door that hears it forgets its controller and waits to be claimed.
Brightlatch, our IT contractor, keeps a test copy: a second main and backup on a laptop, with one door on a bench. It is for trying things without touching the real doors, which they call live.

Tuesday was their first game day: a planned night of breaking something on purpose, to check the system copes. Ifeoluwa's plan sheet gives what she'll do, what should happen, what it may touch, and the stop rule, a sign that ends the test at once:

do:        switch off test backup, 02:10:00
expect:    test main takes over
touches:   test copy only
stop rule: none needed

In the copy, the backup was in charge of the bench door, so switching it off should make the test main take over. Nobody told me. At 02:10:00 she switched it off, and it said 'controller down'. At 02:10:02 the test main claimed the bench door.
At 02:10:30 I heard the big-cat house bolt slide back.

No card. The door gave when I tried it. Through the inner glass, two tigers lay awake in their night dens, behind slides we bolt by hand, watching the door. I held it shut. At 02:12:00 the bolt shot home under my hand.
Her test report: the time, the result, what it touched.
02:10:02  PASS  test main took over in 2 s. Test copy only, no live effect.
The big-cat door's log: the time, what the bolt did, why, and the card.

02:10:00  heard 'controller down', waiting to be claimed
02:10:30  UNLOCKED  no 'all well' for 30 s     card: none
02:12:00  LOCKED    claimed by main, roll call  card: none
All four doors logged the same. The live main never stopped saying 'all well'; the doors had forgotten it. Its roll call had gone out at 02:10:00, just before the test; the next came at 02:12:00.

The test copy has used our only hub every night since it was set up, claiming only the bench door. Its group name was copied from live. It had never been switched off; nor, since fitting, had either live controller. Nobody had drawn what test and live share.

blocks.label: north_hub_0209_0213.png

diagram.aria: 02:09:30 to 02:13:00. The test backup runs until 02:10:00 and is switched off after that. The live main says all well the whole time. The big-cat house keeper door is claimed and locked until 02:10:00, unclaimed but locked from 02:10:00 to 02:10:30, unlocked from 02:10:30 to 02:12:00, and claimed and locked again from 02:12:00.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the door log and the test report. At 02:10:00 the test backup said 'controller down' and the big-cat door forgot the live main, which went on saying 'all well' to doors no longer listening. Thirty seconds of silence later, at 02:10:30, the fire rule unlocked it. The 02:12:00 roll call claimed and locked it.

blocks.text: Everyone followed their rules. What should we change before the next game day?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: A game day like this starts by writing down the steady state, a measurable sign that all is normal, and the hypothesis, the guess that it stays normal while you break something. So: what was Ifeoluwa's steady state, and was it measured on the bench or at your four doors? Before 02:10, who could have told her how far 'controller down' would travel? And at 02:10:10, who was looking at a live door's log?

replies.author: u/quernmoor_nights_nokuthula
replies.text: Her steady state was 'the bench door stays locked', checked on the laptop. Nobody looked at a live log; I learned there had been a test at 06:00. Ifeoluwa says the hub delivers a message to every door with that group name, and she didn't know ours matched. Each pair of controllers watches its partner over a cable, not the hub, so the test main saw its backup go, while the live backup saw nothing wrong with the live main and stayed out of it.

comments.author: u/just_stop_paoletta
comments.text: Your contractor will call this chaos engineering: breaking things on purpose, under control, to learn how the system copes. In a zoo it's reckless. They'll talk about the blast radius, how much a mistake can hit. Here it's a tiger. Before Brightlatch started switching things off, no door ever opened by itself. Just stop. No game day, no ninety seconds of open door. Test software in an office, not in a building with animals in it.

comments.author: u/daylight_drills_szilvia
comments.text: Game days are fine; 2 AM is the problem. Run them at two in the afternoon with the whole IT team on site and a keeper at every house. Someone would have seen that door within seconds, and nobody has to explain a bolt to a night keeper who wasn't told.

reply.prompt: Brightlatch has asked for another game day next month. What should Quernmoor change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: List what test and live share first, then start with one door and a stop rule.
options.part2: Ifeoluwa and I drew every path between test and live on one sheet. Two joined them: the north hub, and the group name copied from live. Before changing anything, she planned one more game day that touched one live door on purpose: she gave the test copy a group of its own and put the feed store, where nothing lives, in it beside the bench door. Hypothesis: the feed store stays claimed and locked. Stop rule: any live door without a controller for 10 seconds ends the test, and the main sends a roll call at once. I stood at the feed store with its log open. In the sim: at 02:10:00 the feed store heard 'controller down'; at 02:10:10 the stop rule fired, the main claimed it again, and it never unlocked. The other three doors heard nothing. Those ten seconds showed the real weakness: a door forgets its controller when any controller says 'down'. Brightlatch changed the doors to take 'down' only from the controller that claimed them, moved the test copy to its own hub, and wrote it all up. Next month they widen to two doors.
options.senior: A first experiment should be the smallest one that can still teach you something. Write down the steady state where it matters (the live doors, not the bench), map what test and live share, put one live door in scope with someone watching it, and set a stop rule that acts in seconds, well inside the 30 s the fire rule allows. Here it found the real fault, doors trusting any 'controller down', at a cost of ten seconds on a door with nothing behind it. Widen only after each step passes, and write each one up.

options.text: Stop game days altogether; switching things off on purpose put the keepers at risk.
options.verdict: The weakness waits for a real fault
options.part2: Our manager cancelled game days, and nothing else changed. On a night in March, at 03:16:00, the live backup's software locked up and restarted itself, saying 'controller down' to its group as it went, and all four keeper doors forgot the main. Nobody was running a test, so nobody was watching. In the sim, the same fault at 02:10:00 unlocks all four doors from 02:10:30 to 02:12:00, the next roll call; in March their logs read 03:16:30 to 03:18:00. I found the reptile house door unlocked at 03:17 on my round. Paoletta was right that switching things off is a risk. But the doors' weakness was there before Brightlatch, and stopping game days only removed the night we might have found it on purpose, with people ready.
options.senior: Failures happen whether you schedule them or not; a game day picks the hour, the size and who is watching. Stopping them leaves every hidden dependency, here the shared hub and doors that obey any 'controller down', to be found by a real fault at 03:16 with nobody looking. The answer to a risky experiment is a smaller, watched one with a stop rule, not no experiment.

options.text: Run game days in the daytime, with the whole IT team on site and the keepers on watch.
options.part2: Brightlatch reran the game day on a Wednesday at 14:00, with the whole IT team in the workshop and a keeper at each house. In the sim, the same test at 14:10:00 unlocks all four keeper doors from 14:10:30 to 14:12:00, with the zoo open. The IT team watched the test copy's screen, which said PASS. The keeper at the big-cat house saw the door give, held it and radioed, and the team found the shared hub that afternoon instead of at 06:00. People watching helped. But it was still ninety seconds of four unlocked keeper doors, now with visitors twenty metres away, because the test was as wide as before and nothing stopped it.
options.senior: People watching is one part of a safe experiment, and the day can suit that: the AWS guidance wants everyone informed and involved. But the hour does not shrink the blast radius. The test still reached every door through the shared hub, the report still measured only the test copy, and no stop rule ended it. Watching tells you sooner; a small scope and a stop rule keep what you learn from costing ninety seconds of open doors.

options.text: Make keeper doors stay locked when no controller speaks, so silence can't open them.
options.part2: Brightlatch set the doors to stay locked after 30 seconds of silence. In the sim, the same test at 02:10:00 leaves all four doors locked but forgotten until the 02:12:00 roll call, and each logs that the fire rule says it must open. On Thursday the zoo's fire safety adviser read the change and had it reversed the same day: if both controllers die in a fire, a keeper inside the reptile house would be shut in. And the test copy was still on the north hub, so the next 'controller down' would make the doors forget their controller again.
options.senior: When a safety rule and a test collide, the safety rule wins; the test has to change. The fire rule unlocks silent doors on purpose, so a keeper is never trapped when the system dies. Making silence lock the doors moves the danger from animals to people and leaves the cause, a shared hub and doors that obey any 'controller down', untouched.

sim.title: Run the game day on the north hub
sim.lede: You're Nokuthula at 02:09:30, half a minute before the game day. The live main has claimed four keeper doors on the north hub, says 'all well' every 5 seconds, and runs its roll call on the even minute. At 02:10:00 something is switched off and says 'controller down' to its group. A door that hears it forgets its controller, and after 30 seconds without 'all well' the fire rule unlocks it. Pick what is switched off, whether the test copy shares the hub, which live doors its group reaches, a stop rule, whether silent doors unlock or stay locked, and the hour. Then run it a second at a time and compare the test report with the big-cat door's log.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to the 30-second mark as now. At 02:10:30 all four keeper doors unlock, while the test report says 'no live effect'; run to the end and the 02:12:00 roll call locks them. Put the test copy on its own hub: nothing unlocks. Back on the shared hub, scope one door: only the feed store unlocks. Add the 10 s stop rule: caught at 02:10:10, nothing unlocks. Now try the live backup failing with no game day, the same test at 14:00, and doors that stay locked when silent.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke into the big-cat house. The test copy's backup, switched off on purpose, said 'controller down' through the hub it shares with live, using the group name it copied from live. The live doors forgot their controller, and 30 seconds later the fire rule unlocked them until the next roll call. Map what test and live share, then start with one door, someone watching it, and a stop rule.

steps.title: What the doors were told to do.
steps.text: A keeper door follows a few steps. First a controller claims it. Then the door counts 'all well' from that controller only. If it hears 'controller down', it forgets its controller and waits to be claimed again. If 30 seconds pass with no 'all well' from its controller, it unlocks, because the fire rule says a silent system must never trap a keeper. Each step is sensible. Together they mean any 'controller down' heard by a door unlocks it 30 seconds later, unless a roll call comes first.

steps.title: How the test reached the live doors.
steps.text: Trace the message. The test backup was switched off at 02:10:00 and said 'controller down' to its group. The group name was keeper-north, copied from live with every other setting. The hub delivers a message to every door with that group name, and there is one hub. So the bench door heard it, and so did all four live doors. The test main claimed the bench door at 02:10:02. Nothing claimed the live doors until the main's roll call at 02:12:00, so they unlocked at 02:10:30 and locked again at 02:12:00.

steps.title: Why the report said 'no live effect'.
steps.text: A test report can only say what it measured. Ifeoluwa's steady state was the bench door staying claimed and locked, and she measured it on the laptop. The live doors were never in the measurement, so they could not appear in the result. 'Test copy only' was written in the plan before the night, as a belief, and the report repeated it. A steady state has to be measured where harm would show: here, every door the hub reaches.

steps.title: A game day, done the careful way.
steps.text: Chaos engineering runs like an experiment. First write down the steady state, as a number you can watch: every live keeper door claimed and locked. Then the hypothesis: switching off a backup leaves it that way. Then pick the smallest blast radius that can still teach you something: one door, with nothing behind it. Then set a stop rule that acts faster than harm can: any door without a controller for 10 seconds ends the test and calls the roll. Then have people watching, with roles: who runs the test, who watches each door, who calls stop. Afterwards, write it up, fix what it found, and only then widen to more doors.

steps.title: Draw what test and live share.
steps.text: A test copy is only separate if everything it touches is separate. List each thing the test uses: the laptop, the bench door, the hub, the radio channel, the group name, the power, the people. Mark which of them live uses too. Every shared item is a shared dependency, a path from test to live, and here two of them, the hub and the copied name, were enough. Then remove what you can (a hub of its own, a group name of its own) and treat the rest as live: in scope, watched, with a stop rule.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for next month. On the left, the test copy, a test main and backup with the group name test-bench, talks only to its own test hub, which reaches the bench door only. In the middle, the live controllers, main and backup with the group name keeper-north, talk to the north hub, which sends orders to the four keeper doors. The doors obey only the controller that claimed them and still unlock after 30 seconds of silence. On the right, the game-day plan, one door with a keeper watching, feeds a stop rule to the live controllers.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for next month. The test copy has its own hub and its own group name, so its 'controller down' reaches only the bench door. Live doors take 'down' only from the controller that claimed them and keep the fire rule. A game day that touches live names one door, a keeper watching it, and a stop rule: in the sim, caught at 02:10:10 with nothing unlocked.

fix.title: The fix: map what is shared, then one door, a watcher and a stop rule
fix.text: First, draw every path between test and live: here the north hub and the group name copied from live. Give the test copy its own hub and its own group name. Second, write the steady state where harm would show: every live keeper door claimed and locked, read from the doors' own logs. Third, start with the smallest blast radius that can still teach you something: one live door with nothing behind it, the feed store, with a keeper watching it and a stop rule of 10 seconds without a controller, which ends the test and makes the main send its roll call at once. In the sim, that run is caught at 02:10:10 and nothing unlocks; it also shows the doors forget their controller on any 'controller down', so change them to take 'down' only from the controller that claimed them. Tell the night keeper beforehand, write each game day up, and widen one step at a time. The fire rule stays.

limits: A map of what is shared is only true on the day it is drawn. A new door, a second hub or a copied setting adds a path the old map lacks, so redraw it before every game day.
A stop rule only works on what it watches. Ten seconds on the feed store caught tonight's fault; a door outside the watch list, or a harm the rule doesn't measure, would still slip past it.
Small and careful is slower. One door a month means months before the whole north hub has been tested, and a real fault can come first.

rows: The test copy's own change was checked: PASS in 2 s.
All four keeper doors unlocked 02:10:30 to 02:12:00; the report said no live effect.
No test ever switches anything off on purpose.
The hidden path stays: the live backup failing unlocks all four doors with nobody watching.
People watching; the open door is seen in seconds, not at 06:00.
Just as wide: four doors unlocked 14:10:30 to 14:12:00, with visitors in.
Breaks the fire rule: a keeper can be shut in when the system dies. The hub is still shared.
Test copy on its own hub
Tonight's test can't reach a live door: 0 unlocked.
Says nothing about the live doors' own weakness; the live backup failing still unlocks them.

explain.seniorTake: Chaos engineering is an experiment, not a stunt. Write the steady state as something you can measure where harm would show, guess that it holds, then break one thing and look for a difference. The first experiment should be the smallest that can teach you something, with someone watching and a stop rule that acts faster than harm can. Before any of it, list what your test copy shares with live: a hub, a queue, a database, a name copied from live. Each shared thing is a path, and a test report that only measures the test copy can't see along it. Game days add the people: a plan with roles, everyone told beforehand, including the night shift, and a write-up that fixes what was found. Physical safety rules, like a fire rule, outrank the test; if they collide, change the test. And don't stop testing because a test found something. Netflix's Chaos Monkey is the famous example, read in Field Report: Monkeys in Production.

realWorld.title: Principles of Chaos Engineering: the definition
realWorld.text: The site's opening line: "Chaos Engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in the system’s capability", and it goes on to say the capability is to withstand turbulent conditions in production. An experiment, in other words, not breaking things for its own sake.

realWorld.title: Principles: steady state, then a hypothesis
realWorld.text: The first step: "Start by defining ‘steady state’ as some measurable output of a system that indicates normal behavior." The second: "Hypothesize that this steady state will continue in both the control group and the experimental group." Ifeoluwa's steady state was measured on the bench, not at the doors that were hurt.

realWorld.title: Principles: Minimize Blast Radius
realWorld.text: "Experimenting in production has the potential to cause unnecessary customer pain." The site says it is "the responsibility and obligation of the Chaos Engineer to ensure the fallout from experiments are minimized." One door with nothing behind it is that idea at Quernmoor's size.

realWorld.title: Principles: the aim is production
realWorld.text: "Chaos strongly prefers to experiment directly on production traffic." The site treats real systems as the goal, which is why a test copy that secretly touches live is the worst of both: the risk of production with the measurements of a copy.

realWorld.title: AWS REL12-BP05: what a game day is
realWorld.text: AWS's Reliability Pillar says: "Game days simulate events in production-like environments to test systems, processes, and team responses." It also lists among the benefits that game days "can help you identify and address these dependencies", the hidden links between systems.

realWorld.title: AWS: the first game day, and who must know
realWorld.text: "A game day, especially the first one, should involve all team members, and all stakeholders and participants should be informed in advance about the date, time, and simulated scenarios." Among the anti-patterns: "You run a game day, but you don't inform all relevant stakeholders." Nobody told the night keeper.

realWorld.title: AWS: roll back, then write it up
realWorld.text: "If the team observes any negative impact, they roll back the test and remedy the identified issues", and "After the game day, conduct a retrospective session to review the lessons learned." A stop rule is the first half made automatic; the write-up is the second.

asked: How would you run a first chaos experiment?
What is blast radius in an experiment?
interview.answer: I'd start by writing down the steady state as something measurable where harm would show, for example the error rate users see or, in a building, every door locked and claimed, and the hypothesis that it holds while I break one thing. Before touching anything, I'd list what the test environment shares with production: a network hub, a queue, a database, logins, a setting copied from production. Then I'd pick the smallest blast radius that can still teach me something, meaning the least that can be hit if I'm wrong: one machine, one customer's traffic, one door. I'd set a stop rule that acts faster than harm can, have named people watching with clear roles, and tell everyone affected beforehand. A game day is that, planned and rehearsed: a scheduled exercise where a team breaks something on purpose, runs its real response, and writes up what it learned, as AWS's Well-Architected guidance describes. Only after a step passes would I widen it. A story I'd tell: a zoo's IT contractor switched off a backup door controller in a test copy that shared a radio hub and a copied group name with the live doors. The test report said no live effect, while four keeper doors were unlocked for 90 seconds by their own fire rule. One door, a watcher and a 10-second stop rule would have caught it with nothing unlocked.

terms.def: The zoo in this story. Its north hub reaches four keeper doors: the big-cat house, the ape house, the reptile house and the feed store.
The keeper who walks the zoo after closing, checking animals and doors. Nokuthula is Quernmoor's.

A small computer that gives keeper doors their orders by radio. Quernmoor has a main and a backup, in case one fails.
Two controllers kept so one can take over if the other fails, like a spare key. At Quernmoor the live main is in charge and the backup waits.
A radio box that carries controllers' messages to the doors, like a post office for one street. It delivers a message to every door with the group name on it.
The name a controller puts on messages for all its doors. The live doors' is keeper-north; the test copy, copied from live, used the same one.
A controller telling one door 'I'm your controller'. A door obeys, and counts 'all well' from, only the controller that last claimed it.
The message the controller in charge sends every 5 seconds. A door counts it only from the controller that claimed it.
The live main claiming every door again, every two minutes on the even minute, so a door that has lost its controller is never lost for long.
The last thing a controller says to its group as it is switched off. As built, any door that hears it forgets its controller and waits to be claimed.
The doors' safety rule: no 'all well' from its controller for 30 seconds and a keeper door unlocks, so no keeper is shut inside if the system dies in a fire.
A second set of controllers, on a laptop with one bench door, for trying things without touching the real doors. Also called a test environment.
The real system that real people and animals depend on. Also called production. The four keeper doors are live; the bench door is not.
The test copy's one door, a real lock on a workshop bench, used to see what the test copy's orders do.
Quernmoor's IT contractor in this story, which set up and runs the test copy. Ifeoluwa ran its first game day.
A planned exercise where a team breaks something on purpose and runs its real response, with roles, everyone told in advance, and a write-up after.
A game day's plan on one page: what will be done, what should happen, what it may touch and the stop rule.
A sign, set before a test, that ends it at once and puts things back, like a referee's whistle. Here: any live door without a controller for 10 seconds.
What a test wrote down about its result. It can only report what it measured; Ifeoluwa's measured the bench door.
Breaking things on purpose, under control, to learn how a system copes: measure normal, guess it holds, break one thing, look for a difference.
A measurable sign that a system is behaving normally, written down before an experiment. Here, every live keeper door claimed and locked.
The guess an experiment tests. In chaos engineering, that the steady state stays the same while something is broken.
How much can be hit if something goes wrong. Tuesday's test could reach all four keeper doors; one door in scope makes it one.
What a test is allowed to touch, written in its plan. Tuesday's plan said 'test copy only'; the hub made it wider.
Something two systems both rely on, such as one hub, queue or database. A test that uses it can reach the other system through it.
Making the next experiment a little bigger only after the last one passed: one door, then two, then the whole hub.
What a keeper door does after 30 seconds with no 'all well' from its controller. As built it unlocks, the fire rule; the sim lets you try staying locked instead.
The real system that real users depend on, as opposed to a test copy. At Quernmoor it is called live.
Anyone who is affected by, or has a say in, a system or a change to it. At Quernmoor that includes the night keeper.
A common way of doing something that looks sensible but usually goes wrong. AWS lists anti-patterns under each of its practices.
A meeting after an event or exercise to review what happened and what was learned, without blame. AWS asks for one after every game day.
A test copy built to behave as much like production as possible, so a test there means something. It is still not production.
The room where an animal sleeps, behind the keeper area. Quernmoor's tigers' dens close with slides bolted by hand, not by the door system.
A short record after a game day of what was done, what was found and what will change. AWS calls the meeting a retrospective.
A short public statement of what chaos engineering is and how to do it, at principlesofchaos.org, last updated March 2019.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's company that rents out computing and storage.
AWS's published guidance on building systems well, in pillars. The Reliability Pillar covers staying up; REL12-BP05 is its practice on game days.
Netflix's chaos-engineering tool, which gives this case its name. Field Report: Monkeys in Production, later this season, reads Netflix's own post.
The person who checks the zoo's buildings and rules against fire safety law and the fire plan.
An international standard for running information security. Its Annex A lists controls, among them A.8.31 on separating environments.
The control on separation of development, test and production environments. ISMS.online's summary says it works "by isolating development, testing, and production environments."

atWork: Look for any test or staging environment that shares one piece of hardware, one queue, one network or one name with production. It is a common pattern: a staging copy built from production's settings keeps production's queue name, topic or group address, and one day a test message lands in production. Check four things. Have you drawn every path between test and production, including copied settings and shared hardware? Is each experiment's steady state measured on production's own signals, not only on the test system? Does the first run touch the smallest thing that can teach you something, with a stop rule and named people watching? And does everyone affected know it is happening, including the night shift? Physical and human safety rules, like a fire rule on doors, outrank any test: change the test, never the safety rule. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.31 asks for separation of development, test and production environments, which ISMS.online's summary says it achieves "by isolating development, testing, and production environments". A map of what test and production share, each game day's plan with its stop rule, and its write-up are the evidence an auditor will look for, so keep them from the first game day.

recall.prompt: Your team keeps a staging copy of the order system for trying changes. Last night an engineer stopped the staging copy's worker to see what happens. As it stopped, it posted 'worker stopping, hand back your jobs' to the one message queue that staging and production both use, and 300 real orders were handed back and sent twice. The test log says 'staging only, no production effect'. Your manager wants to ban all failure tests. What happened, and what would you do instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Staging and production rely on the same queue, so the test's message reached production; list what they share
Don't ban tests; make the first one as small as possible and widen later
Set a stop rule and have people watching production's own signals

recall.model: The test was not staging only: staging and production use one queue, so the worker's 'hand back your jobs' message reached real orders, and the test log only measured staging. Banning failure tests won't remove that path; the same message goes out the day a production worker crashes. First list what staging and production share and give staging its own queue. Then test the real failure on purpose, with the smallest blast radius that still teaches you something: start small, with one test order on one production worker. Set a stop rule (any real order handed back ends the test at once and you roll back), have people watching production's own numbers, tell everyone beforehand, and widen only after it passes. Also make workers ignore hand-back messages that don't come from their own worker.

recall.prompt: In chaos engineering, what is a steady-state hypothesis?
options: A guess about which part of the system will break first
A measurable sign that the system is normal, and the prediction that it stays normal while something is broken
A rule that ends a test after a fixed number of minutes
A list of every machine the test is allowed to touch
recall.why: The Principles of Chaos Engineering start with steady state, "some measurable output of a system that indicates normal behavior", and then hypothesize that it continues. Quernmoor's should have been every live keeper door claimed and locked.

recall.prompt: Why did Ifeoluwa's test report say 'no live effect' while four keeper doors were unlocked?
options: The live doors only unlocked after the report was written
It measured only the test copy and the bench door, so the live doors were never in its result
The hub hid the live doors' logs from the laptop
The fire rule wiped the live doors' logs
recall.why: A report can only say what it measured. The steady state was checked on the bench door; 'test copy only' was a belief written in the plan. Measure where harm would show.

recall.prompt: What does AWS's Well-Architected practice on game days (REL12-BP05) say about the first game day?
options: Run it without warning anyone, so the response is realistic
Involve all team members, and tell all stakeholders and participants the date, time and scenarios in advance
Run it only in a test copy, never near production
recall.why: AWS writes that "a game day, especially the first one, should involve all team members, and all stakeholders and participants should be informed in advance", and lists not informing all relevant stakeholders as an anti-pattern. Quernmoor's night keeper wasn't told.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Brightlatch moved the test copy to its own hub, and the doors now take 'controller down' only from the controller that claimed them. Game days went from the feed store to two doors, then to all four, each with the 10-second stop rule and a keeper at each door on the plan sheet. In April the zoo opened a nocturnal house; its keeper door came from another maker, and the electrician put it on the north hub. Last night's game day switched off the live backup at 02:10:00. The report said: four doors watched, all claimed, PASS. At 02:10:30 the nocturnal house door unlocked, until the 02:12:00 roll call. Its software still forgets its controller on any 'down'.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the game day miss the nocturnal house, and how should Quernmoor keep its game days safe as the zoo changes?

keyIdeas.idea: The plan's list of doors, the map of what the hub reaches, was out of date: the nocturnal house door was never added
Take the steady state from everything the hub reaches, not from a list typed once
After any change, shrink the blast radius again: test the changed part alone first, then widen

coldCase.model: The game day watched a list, not the hub. The plan sheet's four doors were out of date: the nocturnal house door joined the north hub in April and was never added, so the stop rule couldn't see it and the report counted four doors as all of them. Take the steady state from the hub itself: every door it reaches, read each time, so a door that joins is watched automatically. Redraw the map of what is shared whenever something is added. And after a change, shrink the blast radius again: start small, with the new door alone first and a keeper beside it, before it joins a whole-hub game day. That run would have shown in ten seconds that its software still trusts any 'down', and the maker could fix it before the doors were ever widened again.
